activities.caption: put the electron bookkeeping in order
activities.name: redoxHalfOrder

config.prompt: Zinc displaces copper from solution. Rebuild the bookkeeping, electrons included:
items: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ — oxidation: the metal surrenders
Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu — reduction: the ion grabs them
Add the halves — the electrons cancel
Overall: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu — the displacement as one line
config.why: Electrons lost must equal electrons gained — cancel them and the displacement stands alone.

activities.caption: pair each entry on the potential table with what it buys
activities.name: redoxTableMatch

config.prompt: Pair each entry with its consequence:

pairs.right: tops the scale — rips electrons from almost anything
bottoms it — surrenders electrons eagerly, hence the best batteries
the Daniell cell — about 1.10 V fresh
Mg is the more eager anode — the pair delivers about 2.7 V

config.why: Positive cell voltage means the reaction runs itself — the table is the equilibrium chapter's K, translated into volts.

activities.anchor: charge builds up and current stops within seconds
activities.caption: find the faulty line — what actually crosses the liquid
activities.name: redoxBridgeSpot

config.prompt: A summary of the Daniell cell contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: Current in the wire only — the moving charge never enters the liquid.
Ions carry it through the electrolyte instead.
Cations drift toward the cathode compartment; anions toward the anode.
The salt bridge ferries the electrons across to complete the loop.
Without it, the beakers polarise and the flow dies almost immediately.
config.correction: The bridge ferries IONS, not electrons — it carries the ionic current and cancels the build-up; electrons do all their travelling in the metal wire.
config.why: If electrons could swim, there would be no need for a bridge at all — and the halves could not be separated.

activities.caption: slide to the temperature cryolite buys
activities.name: redoxCryoPlace

config.prompt: Cryolite's whole job is cutting the price of liquefying bauxite's oxide. Slide the marker to the operating temperature that buys.
config.why: About 950 °C, down from 2,072 °C — and the process still draws roughly 14,000 kWh per tonne, which is why smelters sit beside hydroelectric dams.

activities.anchor: reverse the current to reset them
activities.caption: drag the divider across the battery drawer
activities.name: redoxCellCompare

config.prompt: Same redox, two jackets — drag the divider across the drawer:

before.label: primary cell
before.text: Runs one way and retires — alkaline AAs: forcing current back generates gas and heat rather than restored reactants.

after.label: secondary cell
after.text: Built reversible — lithium-ion shuttles Li⁺ between graphite layers and a metal-oxide cathode, surviving thousands of cycles since 1991.

config.why: One chemistry survives the shuttle, the other ruptures — the label on the pack encodes the electrode chemistry, not a charging trick.

activities.anchor: Rechargeability is a design property, not a voltage trick
activities.caption: true or false — batteries and their names
activities.name: redoxBatJudge

statements.why: They store chemical energy whose controlled release is electricity — the mass barely changes while it powers a city block.

statements.s: Any battery can be recharged if you push current in long enough.
statements.why: Primary cells' reactions are not reversible by design — forcing current back makes gas and heat instead of restored reactants.

statements.s: Anode = oxidation and cathode = reduction, always — which one is positive depends on the mode.
statements.why: Discharging: cathode positive. Electrolysing: anode positive. Learn the chemistry, not the polarity.

statements.s: A 'dead' battery is simply one whose redox has run to equilibrium.
statements.why: No difference in pulling power left — the gap between the half-cell potentials has closed.

activities.caption: call the bill for rust nobody ordered
activities.name: redoxRustEst

config.prompt: Rusting eats infrastructure nobody ordered. Roughly what share of national output do wealthy countries lose to it each year?
config.why: An estimated 3–4% of GDP — the largest unintended electrochemistry programme on Earth.
config.context: Salt accelerates the damage by making the electrolyte conduct better — coastal and de-iced roads rust hardest.
